The funds were judiciously applied within 18 months to secure key business events through a competitive bidding process, focusing on the national and international marketplace.

This was particularly crucial during this time when cities like Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver intensified their focus on the national market during the pandemic escalating competition significantly.

Thanks to the strategic development and the deployment of the Civic Hospitality Reserve Fund, Discover Saskatoon has not only sustained but significantly boosted our city's appeal and economic vitality during a critical recovery period for our industry.
The figures speak volumes about the tangible impacts we've achieved.
The events supported by the CHF surplus are projected to generate a remarkable total economic impact of $12,571,000.
This substantial contribution underscores the fund's role in stimulating local business activity and the services that depend heavily on the event driven revenue.
The events we've secured with the aid of the CHF surplus, account for a total of $10,700 and $8 requested room nights.

From 2022 to 2025, these events will bring an estimated 7,275 delegates to the city of Saskatoon.
Each delegate represents a unique opportunity for local restaurants and spending in shops, fostering lasting impressions of Saskatoon that can lead to repeat visits and enhance reputation.

During a time when the meetings and events sector is still striving to rebound, the CHF surplus enabled Discover Saskatoon to act on behalf of the city of Saskatoon competitively, maintaining our relevance in this key sector for our visitor economy.
In closing, while I acknowledge the delay in reporting, I hope that the results speak volumes about the funds impact and efficacy.
Discover Saskatoon remains committed to leveraging every opportunity to bring economic prosperity and social wellbeing to our city.
We look forward to continuing our collaboration with the city of Saskatoon to attract more business events for the future.

7.1.1 is utility billing delivery options, Mr. Hack.
Thank you, Mr. Chair.
This report is in response to an outstanding city council resolution to report back on changing utility bill defaults from paper to e-bill.
As well as the potential to implement a monthly fee for those who still choose to receive a paper bill.
In 2023, the city of Saskatoon spent just over $863,000 for the printing and mail costs related to utility bills.
In addition, Canada Post has proposed a rate increase of 7.61% in 2024, which would increase cost by approximately 56,000 additional dollars assuming 2023 volumes.
The city's current e-bill participation is at 34%, which is a 209% increase over the 11% participation in 2016.
The report outlines several options, including the status quo, making e-bill the default option for customers, additional charges for paper bills and incentives for e-bill sign-up.

In completing a jurisdictional scan, the aid other utility providers have similar policies to the current one at the city of Saskatoon, and that they offer both paper and e-bill options with no financial charges or incentives.

Sass power is the only utility service provider that has e-bill as the primary default billing option, and have seen significant increase in e-bill participation since introduced in 2021, which now sits at 60%.

The administration is recommending option number two, which sets e-bill as the default option for new customers, with the goal of achieving similar results as Sass power over time as new customers register.

Although an incentive or additional charge would likely result in quicker uptake in e-bill sign-up and cost recovery, the administration did not recommend this to be consistent with other utility providers,

7.2.2 is capital project contingency amendment to council policy. Mr. Hacker, we back to you.
Thank you, Mr. Chair. This report is in response to a resolution from December 16th, 2019.
Requesting that administration report back regarding the ability to include contingency amounts in capital projects when requesting approval from city council.
Currently contingency amounts are not shown separately within the city's budget submissions.
Administration would have the ability to include contingency information within a manually input a text line in the budget documents.
However, we are not recommending this as it is not common practice and could impact the city's ability to achieve best value through the city's procurement and contract management processes.
During administration's review of existing policy, it was determined that the current maximum contingency of 10% currently listed within policy may not encompass all scenarios.
For example, unique projects with more risk larger contingencies may be required.

As such, the administration is recommending changes to the city's multiyear business plan and budget policy to allow for more professional discretion and determining the appropriate contingency included within each project based on the risk included.
As always, any unused contingency or project budget once closed will be returned to the original source or reserve upon completion of a project.
